We must view this measure through the eye of the farmer. The farmer will remember the Conservative vision of a few years ago on which the Conservative party campaigned. The farmer will remember that this same hon. gentleman, the present Minister of Agriculture, put before the Canadian people the vision of northern development. He spoke of glorified solutions to the problems of developing the north. He spoke of a city encased in a bubble of glass on the very rim of the Arctic circle. There was no truth or sincerity in that vision. It has not come to pass nor will it do so for a long time.
Some of the minister's suggestions concerning solutions for the problems of agriculture are just as much a pipe dream and a vision as were his suggestions regarding northern development on which the Conservative party campaigned not long ago.
Hon. members of the C.C.F. have always been interested in the advantageous use of agricultural lands. We and all farmers know

Marginal Lands
that much of the land in Canada should never have been put into agricultural production because of unsuitability. It was cleared and developed for agricultural purposes because there was no control or regulation of land development and no advice was given concerning the suitability of land for agricultural use.
Changed conditions have come about. We all know that the accessibility provided by our waterways and transportation systems was a feature in the development and exploitation of some land. It is a tragedy that, because of lack of government supervision and control, much land which should have been left in forest production has been wastefully exploited. This is true of many parts of the Ottawa valley, my own area and parts of northern Manitoba and of other provinces. The government should have given leadership in this regard; and because of our failure to provide leadership in the past we perhaps deserve what has taken place. In my area it is now possible to receive provincial government assistance in putting land into production but the cost of putting such land into production is more than the land would ever be worth.
It is no solution to agricultural problems for the government to say it has a vision of trees growing throughout Canada on land not suitable for agricultural production. The results envisaged by the government will not come about overnight for the simple reason that many people who now depend on revenue from woodlots are not receiving any more income from land put to this use than they would receive if the land were devoted to any other type of agricultural production. In many cases such farmers fall into the category of the 29 per cent who receive less than $1,200, to which group the minister referred this afternoon.
The government has referred to this wonderful solution to agricultural problems but it has taken a strange position. The government has said in effect: "We have a wonderful solution but let us not do anything about it; we will let the provinces do something about it. Let them decide what they will do and we will assist them put it into effect". This government does not have half the guts, vision and authority of the former government which did not have those qualities in too large proportion either. The Liberal administration enacted the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act relating to various phases of agricultural development including community pastures. That government did not ask the farmers, municipalities or provincial governments to contribute to the
fMr. Peters.]
program. That government gave something to agriculture from the federal purse through this program.
In the annual report of the Canadian Department of Agriculture for the year ended March 31, 1960, we read that there are now 64 operating pastures including a total of 1,814,544 acres. By agreement with Saskatchewan and Manitoba, large areas of land unsuitable for cereal crop production are leased to the federal government for the establishment of pasture facilities. Reference is made to individual pastures but little would be gained by such detailed reference here. It is indicated that the number of pasture patrons increased by 496 with 6,331 farmers and ranchers making use of the pastures in the 1959-60 season. Each patron pays a certain amount to the federal government to pasture a certain number of cattle or other animals on the community pasture. The former government inaugurated this program to assist western farmers and develop pasture.
The report also indicates that eight construction and three water development crews carried out an extensive construction and maintenance program on the pastures. In addition to 80 maintenance jobs, the water development crews erected 32 new windmills, dug 38 wells and established 21 dams, 31 dugouts and 16 springs. It is also indicated that regrassing, the construction of stockwatering facilities and irrigation development were the main types of work undertaken in the open plains pastures during 1959; 11,030 acres were regrassed, 14 dug-outs and 19 dams were constructed, and further irrigation development was carried out on eight pasture irrigation projects in southwestern Saskatchewan.
The former federal government inaugurated this program and did not expect the municipalities or farmers to take the initiative. In view of the fact that the present government has not altered the program one may conclude that, on the basis of this government's philosophy, it is not opposed to programs of this nature. It is therefore difficult to understand why the government expects the municipalities, provinces and farmers to take the initiative in respect of the program dealt with in the present resolution.
Let us take an example of what the present government has done. It introduced crop insurance legislation. Under this legislation what did the federal government give to the farmer? It donated 20 per cent of the cost of the program and the balance must be provided by the provinces, municipalities and the farmers. We need badly what is envisaged in the present resolution but we should tell

the farmer he is not going to get much out of this measure. He is going to have to pay for it. He is not going to get any particular assistance from Ottawa. Therefore, I suggest right now we can guarantee that the federal government will probably pay the administration costs of this program but the provinces, the municipalities and the farmers themselves will have to pay a great share of the cost. This is not what should be done. The government should not say, "We want to talk to the provinces and see what they are going to do." The federal government should go out and say, "This is what we will do, and we will do it for any province, any farmer, or any municipality that wishes to meet the terms of the program that we will present to them."
This reutilization of submarginal land through agricultural reforestation is not something that will solve the unemployment problem. If under the program farm land is purchased and the farmer is removed from the land we shall eliminate that farm land from agricultural production and put it into forest production. That will take the farmer oil the land, but it will put him into the evergrowing and increasing ranks of the unemployed. It will bring about two things. It will take the farm out of agricultural production and it will take the farmer out of farming and put him into the ranks of the unemployed. From the short range point of view, this program will not do anything to solve the problem of agriculture or to help the Canadian farmers, particularly the 37 per cent whose average income is less than $1,200. This is particularly true of the next three, four or five years.
May I say I think the minister has not been completely honest in his presentation of this program. I do hasten to congratulate him on having the foresight to assist in two things. One is the setting up of the Department of Forestry. Certainly he is a very influential member of the cabinet, and I think this is going to have a great influence on agriculture. The second is the bringing forward of this particular program, even though I do not think he has shown very much courage because he has not introduced it on a national scale. Instead, he is asking the provinces and the municipalities to do all the initial implementing of the program, with government assistance. He has shown some leadership in this field.
In the winter works program the Department of Labour has asked the municipalities and the provincial governments to do the major share of the work. This is also true of the tax agreements. The federal government has been willing to assist, but it has never been willing to give the initial leader-
Marginal Lands
ship in these things. As to what can be accomplished-and this is not new-I hold in my hand an extract from the Country Guide, which was published last month, I think. There is an article headed:
Managed woodlots earn $15 per acre.
New Brunswick's tree farm program has turned wood into the province's most popular farm cash crop.
The article goes on to talk about a man who has assisted in the operation in New Brunswick. As I say, this program is not new; it has been going on in the province of New Brunswick for some time. I quote from the article written by Don Baron. He is speaking about John Torunski of the University of New Brunswick forestry extension service, and he says:
When he joined the program, he was visited by John Torunski of the University of New Brunswick forest extension service. Torunski is a young man who knows forests and trees thoroughly. He was raised in Quebec and graduated in forestry from the University of New Brunswick. He has studied woodlot management practices in Europe (where certain species of wood are worth up to $300 per cord) and in several provinces across Canada. He is a pioneer in his own way, preaching the gospel of woodlot management with all the zeal any agricultural representative ever brought to farm extension work.
Torunski sees woodlots as an ideal farm cash crop. "Once a well managed woodlot in New Brunswick is in production, it can produce over a cord of wood per acre, worth $10 to $15 annually,'' he says. "One man can look after 100 acres and do the work himself."
He visited a particular farm and discussed the program with the farmer. The article goes on to say:
On this visit, he also inquired about Dunphy's farm program, because the woodlot and the farm must complement each other if they are to be successful. He talked over long term goals with Dunphy.
The article goes on:
"No two woodlots are the same," Torunski explains, "so no two management plans can be the same either."
I shall leave out a paragraph or so:
Commenting on his province's tree farm program, New Brunswick's deputy minister of agriculture, Reg. Gilbert, who played a big part in its success, says that woodlots offer the best hope for many farmers to boost their income. "Woodlots are the most overlooked cash crop I know of," he says. "The average woodlot produces only one quarter of a cord of wood per year-yet it can be made to produce several times that much."
Mr. Chairman, I will not quote any further from this article. I recommend that every hon. member read it and the recommendations which are included in it. They are brief and I should like to read them:
Recommended Woodlot Practices
Walk through every area in the woodlot at least once every 10 years to see what is there. Harvest trees that are ready, especially overmature and dying ones.

Marginal Lands
When working through an area, cut down dead trees as well as those severely infected by disease, even if they can't be sold.
Build a good road system through the woodlot, to save time hauling out wood. Roads should be 12 or 13 feet wide to carry trucks.
Get out and find a market for your trees. Take a few days every year to find out what kind of wood is selling and who wants to buy.
Consider leaving healthy trees standing for a few years, if the market for such species is not good. Markets change quickly, and such trees could be in demand in a few years.
I believe this is the program that has been put into effect. I am sure the minister is familiar with it and has given some consideration to it.
Previous speakers have mentioned that this measure is not going to do anything for the farmers. This article indicates that for a farm to be successful it must be 500 or 600 acres in extent. This program is going to mean that farmers will have to be moved from one area to another, and this can be done successfully. The farmers who remain will be integrated into a woodlot operation and other types of agricultural production. If this program is to be successful it will have to be supplemented with other types of agricultural operations. This type of development is seasonal and a part-time operation in many instances, and it is meant to supplement other types of farm income.
The hon. member for Halton who just took his seat pointed out that this should not be done. He might be interested to know that under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, in 1959, the federal government carried out a rehabilitation program. I shall read from the annual report to the minister, which I recommend to the hon. member:
Where resettlement was necessary to rehabilitate farm families, farmers were given assistance in moving to irrigated land in Alberta. During 1959, three Saskatchewan farm families were moved to the Hays district of the Bow river project, completing the present phase of the resettlement program. There are now 162 farm families resettled on this project.
I would presume the reason they are being settled there is that the federal government purchased the land and developed it. They are now in a position to say that the land is resettled and production has begun.
This will also have to take place in Ontario, Mr. Chairman. Many of our farmers own farms of 160 acres, with 20 or 30 acres cleared, and they are trying to earn a living from the bush operations as well as from general farm production. These farmers are being penalized as a result of their inability to move from these farms and go into areas where other forms of agriculture are possible. Some incentive to move from such areas will be provided by this legislation. I would suggest that the incentive take the form of expropria-

tion of the farm so the farmer could be paid for that land and the land could be brought under government control. At least we would then be able to plant trees and eventually bring the land into some type of production.
The situation to which I have referred does not apply to those areas in which wood-lot operations are now in effect. The province of Quebec has been doing this type of work for years. The agriculture representatives in that province have gone to the farmers and advised them about these operations. However, in Ontario it will be necessary for the federal Department of Agriculture to set up experts in woodlot operations who will be able to give the farmers advice in silviculture and pest control and other forms of assistance in connection with these operations. This will have to be done on a federal basis. No longer will it be necessary to request the government of a province to undertake such a program, even with federal assistance.
There is another form of assistance that can be given, and that is in connection with the growing of Christmas trees. In 1957 Canada produced 12 million trees which were exported to the United States. These trees had a total value of $6,240,000 or an average of 52 cents per tree. Consumption in the United States had a total value of something over $45 million. It seems to me that many areas of Canada are in a good natural position to take advantage of this market for trees. However, this form of assistance will not be given by merely telling the farmers they can plant as many trees as they like because the trees will be supplied free. The December issue of the "C-I-L Oval" contains an article outlining the methods to be followed in planting these trees and in running such a plantation. The article states:
Under the plantation method, trees are planted in rows six feet apart, that is approximately 1200 trees to the acre, and they are ready for harvesting when they reach a height of six or seven feet. However, special types of trees must be chosen for growing in this manner.
The article then goes on to outline the different types of trees that should be used.
Many of the farmers in northern Ontario, Mr. Chairman, are now engaged in the business of pulpwood production. The hon. member for Halton said that we did not need government controlled marketing boards. He said we did not need government interest in this particular aspect of the problem. Let me tell him that if the government is not interested in this aspect of the matter I would strongly advise the farmer to stay out of pulp-wood production because he is not getting anywhere near the value of his production. The manager of one of the larger paper companies in Canada said that it was costing his

company $40 per cord for pulpwood delivered to the door of the mill from the company's limits. At the same time the farmers in the surrounding area were being paid only $12 to $18 per cord for delivering their pulpwood to the door of that same mill. It seems to me that before we ask the farmer to take part in this large reforestation program we should be able to assure the farmer that he is going to receive a fair price for his products. Perhaps the farmer should be given some type of cooperative organization through which the producers would be able to get together and assure themselves of a much better price for their products than they are receiving now.
I have always been told how backward Ontario was in the development of agriculture. Perhaps the politicians have been saying this. I was surprised, therefore, to find that, according to the figures the minister quoted a while ago, 47 per cent of the farmers in Quebec received less than $1,200 a year as compared with 29 per cent of Ontario. These figures would indicate to us that the farmers in Quebec were not getting a very fair deal either. I am told that the province of Quebec has established government boards which market the pulpwood for the farmers. As a result of this procedure the farmers have been receiving as high as $28 per cord for their pulpwood in the area of Quebec which is just across from my riding. This price should be compared with the $12 to $18 per cord received by the farmers in northern Ontario.
It is all very well, Mr. Chairman, to say that this really does not matter and that this is not a field into which the federal government should enter. This resolution, however, does something for which we have been asking for a long time. This program can be advantageous to the farmer. I feel it is the responsibility of the federal government to do something to ensure the farmer of a market which will give him a reasonable reward for his effort in producing his crops. The minister will have to give consideration, first of all, to the need for the extension of services to woodlot operators. At the moment we have no federal agricultural representatives engaged in this type of educational program. We need agriculture representatives who will go around to the farms to discuss problems that will arise in connection with these operations, much as the provincial agriculture representatives do. The provincial representatives have set an example which the federal government will have to consider.
I believe the minister will have to reorganize his department. I understand the deputy minister will be moved very shortly
Marginal Lands
and there will be a shake-up in the department that will permit the reorganization of that department. This reorganization should be done bearing in mind some of the better things that have happened in the provincial departments.
In addition, I believe that we need to supplement this reforestation program with a program for agricultural production. This is not a short term program; it is not something that will solve the problems of agriculture in Canada tomorrow or even 10 years or 15 years from now. The reforestation program has to be supplementary to good farm practices in other fields of endeavour. It could be supplementary to dairy production, for instance. It can supplement all the other forms of agriculture that farmers are now depending on. This can be an additional form of cash support. If we hold out the idea to farmers that they are going to be able to combine their farms with their neighbour's farm under one woodlot and make a living next year, I think we are misleading them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, in introducing this resolution in the house on January 26 last the Minister of Agriculture detailed three types of operations which would be the basis on which the federal government, in co-operation with provincial governments, hopes to make agricultural rehabilitation and development a reality. Briefly they are projects for the alternative uses of land which are presently classified as marginal or of low productivity; projects for the development of income and employment opportunities for rural agricultural areas; and projects for the development and conservation of the water and soil resources of Canada.
This is just another step forward in the government's agricultural program as enunciated by the Prime Minister in 1958. Personally I believe this is a very important part of that program and I believe this view is shared by most hon. members in this house, because we are beginning to realize that rural development and conservation is one phase of our national life that we Canadians have been prone to disregard, even though it involves our most important national resources of soil and water.
Though we consider ourselves as a highly developed nation, with the knowledge and the techniques available to a modern society we continue to neglect to a great extent the lessons learned from past civilizations which refused to recognize the impact that

Marginal Lands
neglect and exploitation of these two resources had on their survival. There was some excuse, perhaps, in the early settlement of the nation for cutting down some of our magnificent forests in order to populate our vast country, or for putting to the plow thousands of acres of natural pasture-land in the scramble to settle our western plains. There is no excuse for continuing this practice in this enlightened age, or for neglecting any opportunity to restore nature's cover to our natural forest and grass areas. The incidence of flooding has been rising notably in the past decade, and many of our fertile valleys, and even some of our industrial areas, are subject to recurrent floods because the natural cover, which in the past had slowed up the melting of the snow in the spring break-ups, has over the years been destroyed.
As important as the soil is to our society, water is probably the most abundant and and widely distributed natural resource throughout the world. Used intelligently, these two great resources complement one another to the greatest benefit of mankind. But in spite of the great abundance of water and our absolute dependence on it for survival, it is today our most wasted, most polluted, and most generally abused natural resource. Fortunately it cannot be destroyed. We cannot destroy it, but that does not mean that we do not have the responsibility to protect, control and conserve it.
One of our western farm papers, the Manitoba Co-operator, described the need for conservation in a recent editorial entitled "Conservation Need Grows". This article reads in part as follows:
The need for soil, water and forest conservation is becoming more and more apparent each year, and is one of the major responsibilities facing the people today. A very impressive amount of work on conservation projects has been done and is being done, but far too many do not realize the ever growing importance of such undertakings. The work is not only for the practical and technical men who are engaged in the various conservation projects, but must receive wholehearted support from people in all walks of life. All must fully grasp the importance of such undertakings to arrest deterioration of soil, water and forest resources. They must realize a nation lives off the land, and play their part by helping to publicize and urge greater efforts in conservation work.
The article continues briefly as follows:
History has long revealed that the wealth of any nation deteriorates with its soil. Once fertile lands along the Mediterranean coast of northern Africa are now desert wastes. Lebanon's cedars went with the soil. Eroding soil is reducing productive areas in many sections of Africa. Australia's black blizzards in the war years were comparable with those that swept out the dust bowls of the south west United States and western Canada in the drought years of the disastrous 30's. It is difficult for people in Canada, particularly those who did not experience the 30's, to visualize such scenes in

this country for future generations, as those that existed in once productive areas now laid waste in other parts of the world. It cannot be too strongly emphasized that soil deterioration in particular in many parts of Canada, is now occurring at a rapid pace. The area of productivity can diminish speedily.
Hon. members will know, of course, that with the exception of our navigable streams, water is a provincial resource, the prime responsibility of the provinces. But, if we are to meet this problem of conservation of our land and water resources as it applies to rural development and diversification of industry, it must be a co-ordinated effort of all levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal and with the federal government, with agencies set up under this act, and perhaps in the western provinces through prairie farm rehabilitation, supplying advice, technical and financial assistance to provincial and local administrations.
In the province of Manitoba, though we have abundant supplies of water, the larger portion of it is in the northern half of the province, remote from the major concentration of our population. Even in the case of the relatively smaller bodies of water in the southern more populous areas, we quite often find the most likely source of water many miles from the desired point of use. Owing to our geographical location and climatic cycles, we have been accustomed to receiving our natural water in varying rates and volumes, both annually and over cycles of years. As an example, the Assiniboine river, one of our major but typical southern streams, can have as much as 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the total annual flow pass a given point on the river in a single month in the break-up period. It also has had as little as 1 per cent pass the same point in the single month of February. Also during the five-year period 1952 to 1957 over seven times the volume of water flowed through this river as flowed in the same length of time between 1936 and 1941. The same situation can be said to prevail on the Souris, the Pembina and other lesser streams. Thus under natural conditions we have floods in the spring and low water, or perhaps no flow of water, during the fall and winter.
As our population increases it is becoming increasingly more difficult, under those conditions, to provide modern sewerage facilities in our rural towns even though recent developments in disposal systems such as lagoons have made it financially possible to dispose of our sewage and industrial wastes without polluting our natural streams. This situation also makes it difficult, or almost impossible, for our rural communities to take advantage of any industrial development, in spite of the fact that there is no lack of

other facilities such as power, roads, transportation, communications, excellent schools and hospitals, and a potential labour force. With only one sixth of our urban population enjoying proper sewerage facilities, a long step forward in correcting this situation was made in the recent budget when funds were made available toward helping finance sewerage installations and proper disposal systems.
I submit that it is of equal or even greater importance that the federal government, in co-operation with our provincial and municipal governments, impound our flood waters, control our streams and provide reservoirs for sewage, industrial development and recreation. Owing to Manitoba's topography in relation to other parts of the continent, water flows into that province from Ontario on the east; from Montana, South Dakota, North Dakota and Minnesota on the south; and from Saskatchewan and Alberta on the west. All this water is on its way to Hudson's bay and the Atlantic ocean.
Since almost all Manitoba's flood control and water conservation projects involve either interprovincial or international waters, participation in these projects involves all levels of government. The federal government has participated with the provinces in a hydrometric service measuring and recording stream flows and lake levels. This is done in order accurately to determine actual water resources and so that watershed development programs and works can be properly planned and designed.
The federal government has also assisted rural development and rehabilitation through the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, in constructing small agricultural dams and dug-outs and in the development of community pastures. I would hope that under this new rural development scheme this phase of development will be continued and expanded to include dams for industrial and recreational purposes for our smaller rural centres.
The rural areas are now requiring water in increasing volume for town supply, for diversification and production through irrigation of crops that would decrease the acreage sown to cereal grains, for food processing, industrial plants and many other purposes. Without it, diversification of industry will remain only a dream to be realized some day in the distant future. Without adequate water supplies and proper control of this important resource, rural development and conservation will be a slow process indeed.
A recent economic analysis made for the Manitoba government, covering south central Manitoba, sets out in detail the agricultural and industrial potential of that region, 90205-6-207
Marginal Lands
as well as recommendations for its development. The 104 page report is entitled "Economic Survey, South Central Manitoba" and is, I believe the first comprehensive survey of its kind made in Canada.
Since it is relevant to the subject under discussion, I should like to quote briefly from the document as it relates to the industrial development, agricultural potential and water conservation for the area. The report states:
Analysis of the productive capacity of south central Manitoba indicates considerable increase in industrial development is possible. Compiled data indicates that the products of increased economic activity are marketable. There is every indication that the people of the region desire such development. It is therefore recommended that the several communities within the region, working individually and in co-operation with one another and with the provincial and federal governments, embark upon a co-ordinated development program.
Such a program will have as its goals the increase of primary agricultural production, the increase of manufacturing and processing, and the orderly economic and physical assimilation of increased population and physical facilities. This, in turn, will require improved patterns of land use, improved and developed conservation and use of the water resources of the area, improved social and administrative organization, and improved urban land use planning.
Feasibility studies of irrigation in Manitoba are now under way. In some areas, especially along the banks of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, some irrigation has been practised successfully. Experiments at the Morden experimental farm have similarly demonstrated satisfactory results from irrigation. Producers of canning crops in the south central region have suffered some drought losses and canners have been somewhat disturbed by quality fluctuations caused by temporary rainfall shortages. As a result considerable interest has been stimulated in the possibility of supplemental irrigation for certain areas of Manitoba, most of which lie within the south central region.
The Pembina triangle-Red river district presently suffers from a shortage of water for domestic, municipal, industrial and agricultural use. Even as late as last week a disastrous fire in the town of Winkler, one of the growing industrial towns of the area, swept through a good part of the main business section. Though three or four fire engines from neighbouring areas came to help the Winkler fire service, they ran out of water-they were pumping from the artesian wells-and the result was that instead of the fire being confined to one or two buildings the whole of one side of Main street was practically burned down.

Marginal Lands
The report to which I have referred goes on to state:
It is anticipated that between 6,000 and 10,000 acre feet per year of water in excess of present use will be required by 19B1 for domestic, municipal and industrial water supplies. During the same period, a demand for water for irrigation may be created. The engineering feasibility of conservation of the waters of the Pembina river has been established, and water from this source would be adequate to meet the anticipated demands. If these demands are not met. the economic development of the Pembina triangle area will be impeded. Control and conservation of the waters of the Boyne river are essential to the development of the town of Carman in the surrounding community.
Should large demands develop at Carman for water to be used either for industrial or agricultural purposes, a proposal has been made to divert water from the Assiniboine river into the headwaters of the Boyne. Further on, the survey states:
The possibility exists of the development of a major tourist resort in the Spruce woods forest area north of Holland, Manitoba, if the proposed dam on the Assiniboine river is constructed.
In summary, the survey indicates that if the proposed development of water resources is carried out the area can expect a population increase of 50 per cent in 20 years and the establishment of at least 40 new industries.
I would respectfully submit to the minister and the government that the P.F.R.A. administration or an agency established under the present measure be given an active role in assisting provincial and local governments in making available to our rural areas adequate supplies of water together with a proper system of flood control. Many of these projects would be financially self-liquidating and though beyond the immediate resources of the communities directly concerned would become a tangible national asset. The intangibles would be in human betterment.
The success of any rural development program depends more than anything else on what we do with our two greatest resources, soil and water. Our hopes for the success of such a program is the recognition by the leaders in our rural areas of its importance. They are looking to all levels of government for co-operation, assistance and guidance in its fullest development. This measure recognizes the importance of conservation to our national well-being and gives us an opportunity to face up to the very urgent problem of rural rehabilitation. It should provide us with the incentive to nurture our natural resources not only for our own advantage but for the benefit of future generations.
In the interests of our national well-being, I hope that with the passage of the bill based on this resolution these objectives can be realized.

We listened to the minister when the resolution was first debated on January 25. We listened to him today, and as far as I can tell he has yet to divulge the main features of the bill which will follow the passage of this resolution.
There is a need-and no one has disputed it-for a redevelopment program for agriculture in Canada. The minister has emphasized-correctly, I think-that there are large parts of the agriculture industry which live at a subsistence level. I submit that this particular legislation will do very little as far as they are concerned. It is a long term measure. It may result in the long run in an improvement of the incomes of people in the lower brackets but I suggest the main reason why this may be accomplished is that the government will succeed in what is the unstated purpose of this resolution, namely moving a large proportion of these people off the farms. They are being squeezed off in the ordinary course of events. Probably this measure will accelerate the movement of farmers from the farms because it is designed to bring about more economic units and that in turn will mean a smaller farm population.
Before the resolution passes I should like to ask the minister whether he will give us some idea as to what proportion of the moneys involved will be paid by the federal government. I think that is a fair question. I think it should be answered. I think the committee has a right to know before this motion passes at least the general range of contributions which the federal government is prepared to make.
Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which was passed some 25 years ago for precisely this purpose, as far as the tremendous development of community pastures is concerned, almost the total cost has been paid by the federal government. We wonder whether the present measure will mean the removal by the government of this kind of proportionate payment. I express the hope and I make the request that the government will do much better under this scheme than it did under crop insurance, because unless the federal government is prepared to pay more than 20 per cent this will be in a large degree a window-dressing measure designed from the beginning to have very rough going. I hope this is not another instance of the federal government trying to slough off a substantial part of its responsibility on to the provincial and municipal governments.
I think it is an affront to parliament for the minister not to give us this kind of information. He wants us to pass this motion, so he tells us, and then he wants to go carpet-bagging across the country talking to the ministers of agriculture and working out

some kind of formula or scheme. Then, presumably, he is going to put this into a bill and ask parliament to approve it. I think the minister owes it to the committee to tell us at least in general terms what he hopes to put before the provincial governments.
I think this matter has not been handled in the best possible way. I think the government's method of handling the crop insurance scheme was the worst possible way, because, before they had discussed it with the provinces at all, they brought in a measure and said to the provinces, "If you want to cooperate you can do so". It is not a measure which has done very much to aid in the field of general crop failure protection. The fact of the matter is that a very small proportion of farmers qualify to come under that scheme. One of the main reasons for that is that the federal government is bearing such a tiny proportion of the cost of the scheme, namely 50 per cent of the administrative cost and 20 per cent of the premium, but not even 20 per cent of the losses or 20 per cent of the liabilities. So I ask the minister if he will tell us whether the government is going to do better under this program than they have done in connection with crop insurance.
Another thing I should like to hear from the minister is this, and I am sure he will be able to answer this question. I want to know whether this measure will in any way supplant the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I wish to know whether the community pastures will be maintained in future as they are now. I also wish to know whether the stock watering schemes and the building of dugouts and stock watering dams will be continued under that act. I ask those questions for what I think is a good reason. Under the legislation to which I have referred the federal government has assumed the major responsibility. The provincial governments initially provided the land by one means or another. In some cases the municipalities provided the land or the farmers provided it by exchanging land for certain other land.
The federal government set up the pasture scheme, put in the fences and seeded some of the land to grass. The whole scheme is now operating under the federal government. It is operated very much like a crown corporation. The scheme may not be entirely self-liquidating and may not recover all its costs but certainly the major part of the expenses are covered by revenue.
I have in my hand the report of the prairie farm rehabilitation branch of the Department of Agriculture for 1958-59. On page 80 it sets out that in 1958-59 there was an area of 1.8 million acres in pasture. The total construction cost had been $5.5 million. There were carried some 117,332 units of livestock.
90205-6-207i
Marginal Lands
One unit of livestock is defined as one head of cattle, one horse or five sheep. It is stated that the average charge to farmers per unit of livestock was $4.64. This is a good scheme and the farmers have supported it. I hope it will be maintained intact and will not be interfered with by the program under discussion.
I do not wish to be unfair but we must keep in mind that the government has attacked some other crown operations. The Canadian wheat board has been attacked by the feed mill policy of the government. Trans-Canada Air Lines has been attacked by the government allowing Canadian Pacific Air Lines to move in on some of their flights. There is a report that the government is considering ways and means of making it more difficult for Eldorado to operate. Rumours persist-and they are not denied in this chamber-that the government has not yet defined its policy so far as the successful operation of Polymer Corporation is concerned.
I am expressing the hope that nothing will be done by the minister to interfere with the good work of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I ask him again to give the committee some information on the points I have raised.
I also wish to have the following information before the resolution is passed. I want to know the minister's estimate of the cost of this measure within the coming fiscal year and I should like him to give a forecast of the cost for the years ahead if he can make that projection.
It has been reported in the press and elsewhere that the minister is much disappointed about the amount of money he expects to get for this measure, that he is not going to get large sums of money, that not much money will be put into the scheme. The minister at this time should be able to give us some idea of the amount of money that will be forthcoming by projection in the next year or so under this measure.
When we pass a resolution preceding a money bill we do so under a practice that has grown up because it has been felt necessary for the government, before asking for such a vote, to give the committee some indication of the amount of money involved. This is a money resolution. The minister has said little or nothing about the question of cost. Before the resolution is carried I hope he will give the committee some information on the points I have raised.

Mr. Chairman, as a quick answer to the points raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia let me say this. In answer to the first question about the amount of money that will be put into these proposals by the federal government, let me first point out that there is a great variety of

Marginal Lands
agreements envisaged between the federal government and each of the provincial governments.
As I have made clear in the past, both governments I know will be happy under some of these agreements to co-operate in putting into effect many of these schemes which are entirely self-liquidating. An example of that would be community pastures where the operating expenses are met by the farmers themselves. The farmers like to carry their own load if they are able to do so.
Under another type of scheme for rural development we can refer to the experience in the United States. Neither level of government put in any money or made any contribution beyond that of professional advice and research efforts that went into helping a local development group implement ideas for their self-help programs.
With respect to the alternative land use part of the program where heavy costs are envisaged, this will depend almost entirely on the rapidity with which the provinces wish to push this program. Other factors to be considered are the necessary research that will have to be undertaken and the question of assessing the market possibilities for various alternative uses for the land. All these questions will decide the cost-sharing arrangement between the two governments.
As for the physical projects referred to in the third part of the resolution, I think the usual expectation here is that it will be on a 50-50 basis. Let me read to the committee the recommendation of the minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan, Hon. I. C. Nollet, who gave evidence before the special committee of the Senate on land use in Canada on May 6 and 7, 1959. This may be found at page 218 of the report of that committee. In giving evidence, Mr. Nollet said:
It is suggested that as a basic principle of soil and water conservation programs, the general approach should be on a shared cost or earned assistance basis for the whole cost of a completed project including maintenance in succeeding years.
In our opinion, the federal-provincial agreements now in effect for the construction of the trans-Canada highway provide a form of inter-governmental agreement which could be the general basis for agreements contemplated under the legislation and policy we recommend.
It is also respectfully suggested that a proper role for the senior government would involve mainly:
1.	Provision of financial assistance in connection with agreed upon projects, on an approved basis.
2.	Making top level technical and professional advisors and consultants available, as requested by the province.
This, in essence, is the type of financial agreement I think we may expect, as put forward by the minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan.

The second point raised concerned community pastures, dugouts, et cetera. I do not think there is any question about this. In the alternative land use portion, this program has as its purpose not only the carrying out of the present program under P.F.R.A. but also the carrying out of a program which will accomplish as much in the next two or three years as was accomplished in the last 25 years under P.F.R.A.
In other words, in the last 25 years, under P.F.R.A. 1.8 million acres have been put to community pasture in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. We are thinking of proposing to the western provinces at least an additional 1 million acres in the next two or three years. If we can get more and there is use for it I would certainly go after it because, as the hon. member for Assiniboia and other hon. members know, there is tremendous overcrowding on the pastures that now exist.
The farmers want this type of diversified use of their land. It enables them to diversify their wheat economy, by being enabled to pasture their cattle on community pastures. As the hon. member said, the cost to the two governments is divided in this way. The provincial government buys the land. We pay the capital cost of preparing it for pastures, providing the bulls and so on. The costs of the operations of the pastures are borne by the farmers. The farmers find this a very acceptable arrangement. They hope that it will not only be continued but will be tremendously stepped up in pace.
I might point out that so far as dugouts are concerned, last year some 4,000 dugouts were built. This year we expect the construction will be about the same, probably 4,000. This is a tremendous program.
The final question was, what was the projected cost of the whole program? I do not think a living person, either in Ottawa or in any other place in Canada, can give an accurate estimate. I have used figures of $300 million to $600 million for the next 10 years to 20 years. I have no way of knowing whether these figures are accurate because I have no way of knowing on the physical side, and on the alternative land use side, the number of projects that will be brought under this plan.
This brings me to the final statement, and this has to do with philosophy. It was suggested by the hon. member for Timiskaming that we should just go ahead as a government and ram these things down the throats of the various provinces and municipalities as we were supposed to have done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. This goes against the grain entirely of myself personally and I think of most people in Canada. The idea

here is that property and civil rights belong to the provinces. The provinces have the responsibility for their farmers in those areas. All we are doing is going to the provinces and suggesting that we enter into a co-operative program. They know the needs of their people as well as anyone. If we can share this program in any form and work out an arrangement that will be satisfactory to both of us, we will do it. I think the idea that is spreading across Canada of a centralized force under the Minister of Agriculture to impose things on people that are good for them, whether they want them or not is a philosophy that is foreign to myself and to most people in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the last statement of the minister I would suggest that what I said was not to ram these things down the throats of the people. Now may be the time to talk about what happens to agriculture in Ontario, for instance. The farmers in Ontario have needs similar to those of the prairie farmers in so far as community pastures are concerned. We get no benefit whatsoever from that type of legislation. Frankly, we would not suggest that this type of thing be curtailed in the west, but that it be extended into Ontario.
What I contemplated, Mr. Chairman, and what I would ask the minister to consider, is the government buying up certain lands in Ontario which are now very cheap. There are farms in my part of the country consisting of 10,000 acres which could be bought in a block. The cost of that land would be probably less than one tenth of the initial cost of clearing it. The government would own the land and have control of it and would supervise the putting of it back into production for the benefit not only of itself but of the country in general.
Community pastures made up of this type of land seem to have worked very well; they worked so well that the minister now indicates that he is willing to double them. What I am suggesting is that this land was put into community pasture because it was of no value to anybody else and nobody was able to make a living on it. There is a great deal of land in Ontario at the present time that is not being lived on; no one wishes to do anything with it. Crops have not been grown on it. Even those areas that have not been deserted very long are in this position. Even the hay is not being cut and no pasturing is being done on it. This is the type of program that the federal government could go into.
If we are going to ask the farmers of Canada in general to support something that
Marginal Lands
the minister as a federal member will recommend but will depend on the provincial governments to decide whether it is going to be put into effect or not, it may well be that the government of Ontario would not be interested in the scheme. It may well be that the province of New Brunswick, which already has this type of development, would be willing to put a concrete area under control and into this type of agricultural reforestation and that the people of New Brunswick may get a very large benefit from it, and yet the people of Ontario, who would like to see something done about the reclamation of land which is not being used for agricultural purposes, would get no benefit at all simply because the provincial government will not go ahead with it.
Certainly we want to protect the property rights of the people. I am not sugesting that the land be expropriated. The land of which I am speaking has a very low sale value at the present time and expropriation, as conducted by the government now, would take this fact into consideration. Large tracts of land could be bought up for national utilization, and this would entail no hardship to anybody. This land would be put into production on a national basis, and full consideration would be given to all provinces. Other provinces would get benefits that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act gives to the western farmers. Mr. Chairman, my first words in speaking on the agricultural estimates are to express my appreciation to the former minister of agriculture for the important legislation that he was responsible for implementing during his term as minister of agriculture. I also wish to compliment the present Minister of Agriculture on his appointment to this important post. It was my pleasure a few years ago to attend a conference with the hon. gentleman and at that time I was intrigued by his knowledge and understanding of the problems facing farmers. I am particularly pleased that he now occupies a position which will enable him to implement some of the ideas he gained from that conference.
My remarks at this time will pertain to the agricultural conditions in western Canada with which I am quite familiar and I hope hon. members will not think that I am being sectional in my outlook because we have hon. members from other areas in Canada who are well qualified to speak of the conditions in the regions they represent. While reference has previously been made to measures taken by this government to reduce the disparity between costs of production and prices received by farmers for their products, I think I could enumerate a few of them again without being accused of boastfulness. For instance, there are the increase in compensation to livestock producers for cattle slaughtered in the control of contagious diseases; cash advances on farm-stored grain free of interest; the amendments to the Veterans' Land Act to enable veterans to obtain increased loans; the greatly improved Farm Credit Act; the long-awaited amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which have removed many of the inequities in the making of payments and broadened the coverage; the acreage payments to western farmers amounting to over $82 million; and the provision of funds through the Colombo plan on long terms to assist India and Ceylon to purchase wheat and flour.
I feel I should also make reference to the recent sale of wheat to China and the opening of an office in Tokyo, Japan, whose main function it will be to promote the sale of grain; and the announcement by the Prime Minister that jurisdiction over the Canadian

wheat board and the board of grain commissioners be transferred from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Agriculture. I feel certain that this action on the part of the government will prove to be of inestimable value to grain producers in the coming years owing to the fact that the marketing of grain is so closely associated with the Department of Agriculture.
I have referred to only a few of the items of legislation that have been enacted by this government to assist agriculture. I am certain that western farmers are encouraged by the action of the government to implement a comprehensive agricultural policy that will enable farmers to help themselves. However, farmers are still confronted with the cost-price squeeze. This particular kind of squeeze has come about because the farm industry's costs are rising steadily and the prices which farmers receive for their products are still falling; hence the squeeze. As hon. members know, I have not made many speeches in this chamber and I am only prompted to do so now owing to the inequitable position in which agriculture finds itself. It is reasonable to expect that the financial position of farmers in the federal constituency of Dauphin is similar to that of farmers throughout the prairie provinces.
The present position of agriculture is not one that has developed since this government took office; rather it is the result of steadily increasing costs of production and the low prices for agriculture produce received by farmers since world war II. The problem had its beginning during world war II partly as a result of the British wheat agreement entered into by the Liberal government. A paragraph from the Searle Grain News of May 7, 1958, explains the situation as follows:
The unwinding of the wheat marketing problem in the future is going to require not only the patience, courage and understanding of all concerned, whatever their personal views, but also a willingness on the part of the Canadian taxpayer to accept, if necessary, any temporary financial burden that may arise. Such a burden, since the early days of world war II, has been shouldered by the western wheat grower, for the benefit of the Canadian people at large. Before long, perhaps, it may be necessary for the population as a whole to assume some part of it.
Another problem closely associated with agriculture is that of unemployment which is so frequently mentioned in this chamber. It seems to me that when we are looking for markets for the products of our factories to help the employment situation, we are overlooking our most important market here at home. By increasing the purchasing power of our farmers, we would create employment all

along the line from the mines to the railroads to the factories back to the transportation systems and offices, et cetera.
While farmers are usually regarded as producers, they are also the largest purchasers of goods of all kinds of any segment of our society. As further evidence of the recognition of farmers as an important market, I will quote from a submission made to the government on June 25, 1958 by a delegation of unemployed from Ontario and Quebec. They suggested an imaginative trade policy for moving wheat that would include long term credits to enable such countries as India, Asia and Africa to buy Canadian grain. In their brief they went on to say:
Call it subsidization if you will, but at least it is priming the most necessary pump-our farm economy. Restore purchasing power to the farmers, and you have gone a long way toward restoring it across the nation.
Let me refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister as quoted on page 42 , of Hansard:
Those of us from western Canada know something of what the result was when the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were devastated when drought hit us to such an extent that there was no purchasing power among the farmers, that there were no jobs in eastern Canada.
The farmer is sometimes underestimated in his value as a market for industrial products which find their way into his operation. According to the economics division of the Canada Department of Agriculture there are more than one million cars, trucks and tractors on Canadian farms and their annual expenses, excluding depreciation and financing, are more than $400 million. About 11,000 tons of pig iron go annually into the making of agricultural implements, and the implement manufacturing industry gives work to more than 10,000 employees, with a payroll of over $42 million. Farmers use $20 million worth of electric power annually and pay nearly $200 million for hired labour. They buy 900,000 tons of fertilizers valued at nearly $70 million, and they use over 600,000 tons of limestone. The cost of pest control each year amounts to $20 million. Farm operating expenditures and depreciation total $1.9 billion annually.
Moreover, an estimated one eighth of the total revenue from motor transport of commodities and about one fifth of the revenue from all carload freight involve agricultural products. The combined revenues total more than $225 million. Hundreds of millions of dollars are spent annually on the construction, maintenance and furnishing of half a million homes owned by farmers. With 17 per cent of the population living on farms, additional hundreds of millions are spent for clothing, recreation, health and education.
