In 1958 there were over 9,000 establishments with more than a quarter of a million employees processing products of Canadian farm origin. The value of products from these establishments amounted to more than $4.5 billion, and the payroll of the employees was $763 million. While the number of farms declined from more than 700,000 to fewer than
600,000	between 1924 and 1958, this reduction was about equal to the increase in the number of employees processing or manufacturing products of farm origin. In addition to these, there are about 70,000 engaged in the food wholesaling and retailing.
I mention these statistics in order to indicate to hon. members the potential market we have in Canada if farmers have the purchasing power. I have had a large number of requests from farm organizations during the last few years for the government to take some positive action to reduce the disparity between costs of operation and prices received for agricultural produce. My own experience as a practical farmer indicates to me that these requests are fully justified. We frequently hear complaints about the costs of support for farm produce, and I would suggest to those who complain that the cost of supporting secondary industry in this country is high by protecting industry through tariffs. In a study of tariff costs made by a Yale economist for the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects, the cost of tariffs to Canadians was estimated at from $610 million to $735 million annually. When Canadians are willing to spend such a large amount to support industry, they should not complain about the small amount the government spends in assistance to agriculture.
As further evidence of the importance of government assistance to agriculture, I wish to quote at this time a statement by Prime Minister Macmillan of the United Kingdom, on June 21, 1960:
A system of price guarantees is not a subsidy to agriculture. It takes the place of tariffs by which manufacturing industry is helped by the government. British farming prosperity has been built up and will be sustained in the future by price guarantees. No country can be truly prosperous without a strong and healthy agricultural industry.
Let me repeat that there are many signs that the decline in western farm income has been a significant factor in causing the unemployment situation in the rest of Canada. I hope that this government will make whatever provisions are necessary to ensure that adequate returns are received by the farmers in the future in order to enable them to share in the general prosperity of Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very brief reference to the new system instituted last year in connection with the deficiency payments on hogs and eggs.

Supply-Agriculture
While we realize the difficulties confronting
the government under the offer to purchase method which created surpluses, the deficiency payment method has not provided the stability in western Canada that was expected. At intervals during the year the price would fall below the prescribed price, but owing to the higher price prevailing in eastern Canada the western producer would not qualify for deficiency payments. Now that the deficiency payment method has been in operation for over a year, I would recommend that the minister take a close look at the disparity in prices prevailing in western Canada with a view to working out a more equitable system in establishing floor prices for these products.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the past year or so some hon. members, particularly those from western Canada, have disparagingly referred to the fact that I personally and others did not represent a farm area; the reference was particularly to me. I was not sure how extensive was the farming area I represented until the other day I decided to send an inquiry to all the farmers in my riding. I found that, rather than representing a very small farming area, I represented one of the very large farming areas of the country and close to 1,400 farmers. Therefore, in the future I shall make no apology whatsoever for the agricultural speeches that I shall be called upon to make.
Sometimes we forget the extent of the agricultural industry in some of the ridings in Ontario which are not normally considered to be agricultural areas. The other day I spoke to a gentleman who was surprised to learn of the topography of northern Ontario. Probably it would be wise to inform the committee at this time of some of the topographical features of northern Ontario. For years some parts of northern Ontario, particularly the Timmins and Timiskaming areas, were represented by representatives of the mining industry, and a great deal was heard of that industry. Particularly from the managers' point of view and from the company operations side of the picture, and very little was said about the farming areas themselves. One of the reasons why I want to mention the topographical features is a desire to interest not only hon. members and the government in a conservation program for my area and for northern Ontario but also to mention the need for certain conservation measures before a condition develops in that area similar to that which has developed in southern Ontario.
The riding of Timiskaming covers almost entirely the little clay belt. This little clay belt contains about a million and a half

acres of probably the best clay agricultural land in Canada. It is a very level area. The little clay belt resulted from the receding waters of a glacial lake which covered the area from James bay almost to the lower end of the Ottawa river valley. The deep part of the lake, which is now called the little clay belt, is an area extending approximately 100 miles from north to south as far as Cobalt where the triangle narrows very greatly to an area from 100 to 125 miles in width. This land is similar to the prairie lands. It is table land which stretches out for many miles with a very slight elevation. You can see from 70 miles to 80 miles from a given point of land. Because the land was created by a lake and later by a river bed it rises in steps which are probably 200 feet high. In this area, as I have said, there are from 1,200 to 1,400 farmers.
There have been many more. Many of the farms in my area are not being operated at all. Many of these farms could be given over to programs such as the one we were discussing a few minutes ago under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the community pasture program. Hundreds and hundreds of acres of agricultural land which have been cleared at great expense by the original owners are lying idle. This land could be put to use as community pastures because there is an exceptional opportunity in northern Ontario for beef production.
During the last 10 or 12 years the beef industry in Timiskaming has increased greatly. We are now favoured by having several large community sale barns which are providing a great impetus to the increasing beef production. In this respect, I should like to ask the minister if it would not be possible for the department to send a government grader to these sale barns during the time the feeder sales are taking place. In this way a farmer who has bought an expensive bull to improve the standard of his herd could be given an opportunity of obtaining the premium price that should flow from the purchase of the very best animals. The farmers are to be congratulated on the amount of money and effort they have expended in attempting to make this transition from the poor grade of beef that was produced a few years ago, mainly as a result of the disposal of dairy cattle, to the situation we have now where we have some exceptional beef herds. Many of these herds are registered under the pedigree act, and each year they are increasing in stature. I feel that it would be advantageous if the department were to send at least a grader or two to these feeder sales so that the farmer could get the benefit of the premium price for his cattle and the buyers from

southern Ontario would be able to assess the grade of cattle that was being produced in this area.
The numerous dairy farms in this area, Mr. Chairman, supply a market of between
100,000	people and 200,000 people. The market is a limited one, but there is some hope that with new equipment for handling dairy products the market will be extended to include the Sudbury and North Bay areas. In this area we have a creamery that has been operating for 25 years and in every one of those years has received not less than the first grade for all the butter that has been produced. I believe this is an enviable record and one that is difficult to equal or to better. All the other facets of agriculture that go with mixed farming are found in this area. A considerable number of mixed crops are grown in this area. Timiskaming has produced some of the best timothy seed that has been produced in Canada and ribbons and awards can be produced from the various fairs across the country to prove it.
The other seed producers of the area are plagued by the lack of markets and a lack of facilities which should be afforded to seed grain growers for disposing of small seeds. We have a great need for some new thinking in connection with agriculture in my area. The farmers are pleased to note that the government is giving consideration to the extension of woodlot operations and the reclaiming of land to be put into pulpwood production. This is one of the areas in which this type of development can be used to great advantage. The present practices in connection with the disposal of the bulk of the products from these woodlots cause us to be worried about the future. We have found that there has never been any equalizing of the costs of production in so far as the pulp and paper companies and the saw mills themselves are concerned and the prices those companies will pay farmers for their products from the woodlots.
No assistance has been given to farm woodlot operators through research into the utilization of wood products that would come from the farm. As a result, very little secondary industry in the woodworking field has been established in the area. We have seen the disappearance of the large operators in the bush industry, and this leaves only the farmers' woodlots from which to draw these wood products. The lack of a market for these products has led some of our entrepreneurs into the plywood and chipboard industries. These people hope they will be able to utilize the resources of the farming communities, and this would provide the farmer with a cash crop that would be advantageous to him.
Supply-Agriculture
I should like to thank the previous minister of agriculture for answering the call of the people of Timiskaming by treating the outbreak of rabies that plagued the farmers of the district. There was never very much for which I could thank the former minister, but I should like to give him credit for this much. The minister did make the facilities of the department available for the inoculation of pet dogs, cats and other domesticated animals. He made the serum and the facilities available and inoculations were carried out in that area. I am very happy to report that the results have been satisfactory. I would recommend to the new Minister of Agriculture that when there is an outbreak of rabies immediate attention be given to it. A program of inoculation should be carried out by the department in connection with all domesticated animals. I am quite sure the minister will find, as we found in northern Ontario, that the response of the farmers will be very good. Most of the citizens were willing to take their pets for inoculation when it did not cost them anything. This procedure did result in the elimination of the outbreak which could have reached serious epidemic proportions.
It is interesting to note that the outbreak was so serious that more than 40 people in that area had to be treated as a result of contact with animals suspected of having rabies. I understand also that there is some considerable difficulty with rabies in some of the counties of southern Ontario. The federal government is now being asked for some support in paying the claims for some of the animals that were ordered slaughtered as a result of being suspected of having rabies. I would strongly urge the minister to continue this fight to control rabies because it is my opinion that rabies can be controlled if the government shows leadership. During the parliamentary recess I made several trips to Ottawa and discussed the matter with the officials in charge of this department. They were willing to act in this regard and indicated that fewer animals had to be destroyed and that the epidemic was of shorter duration than it would normally have been because of this program.
Timiskaming is famous for many other reasons. The potato king of the world has very often been a man from our area. We have embarked on a program sponsored by local businessmen of inviting farmers from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to come to our area to take advantage of the amount of unused land that we have and the favourable climatic conditions for the growing of potatoes. These men from the maritimes are offered plots of 500 acres or 600 acres for their use and are financed by businessmen on a crop share basis. Profits from such a venture

Sup p ly-A griculture
would be split equally between the farmer and the supporter. This program was commenced on a small scale last fall and I understand it was highly successful. It was so successful in fact that I am sure it will continue on a much larger scale this year. As a result of this program I suggest that the Timiskaming area will develop into one of the largest potato growing areas in the country within a very short period of time. I would suggest that this is a very good area for this type of crop because of the existence of facilities, the availability of land, and its closeness to market. For the reasons I have mentioned I feel that Timiskaming will become even better known as a potato producing area.
It has been difficult for individual growers in our area to retain the potato growing championship because of the fact that these individuals have in past years won this championship two or three times in a row. The officials of the exhibit in Chicago will no longer allow those individuals to enter the exhibit. They have suggested that we should allow someone else to win. Perhaps in the near future we can enter this exhibit and win the championship not only on the basis of quality but perhaps on the basis of quantity as well.
I feel that the Timiskaming area is one of the best farming areas in this country. During the past years we have had very favourable climatic conditions and the farmers have always shown an ability to work hard. The growers in this area were blessed at the beginning because of the relatively low cost of land. They were able, as individuals now are, to carve farms out of the bush. As a result, it has been possible for a strong and forceful farming population to grow. However, I should like to invite some of the western farmers to northern Ontario in order to see for themselves the conditions that exist on some of the farms here. I would suggest to the farmers of western Canada that they should not holler so loud because perhaps the farmers in eastern Canada will decide to ask for some of the advantages presently received by those western individuals. I would suggest they show some sympathy for the eastern farmers and their problems. Surely I do not have to remind them that because of this government they enjoy benefits that eastern farmers do not receive.
We have heard fine-sounding arguments regarding woodlots, and other election propaganda of late; but surely we should not put these arguments on that basis because this situation which exists in eastern Canada is a very important one to the farmers of these areas. One need not travel to northern Ontario to see that there are individuals living on farms and working for very small wages in 
the villages and towns in order to buy and maintain the equipment needed to carry on with the farming operation.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly.
What is the hon. member's specific complaint regarding the difficulties existing among the western and eastern farmers?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would refer the hon. member to the dispute that is taking place in regard to feed grain. We have been informed today that in western Canada the price of feed is 50 cents a bushel less than it is in eastern Canada. This will have the result of western farmers feeding cattle with grain that cost 50 cents a bushel less than the cattle feeders pay for feed grain in eastern Canada. There is a further problem involved in regard to this feeding problem in eastern Canada. It is my understanding that in many cases the farmer in western Canada grows the feed and takes it to the feed mill where it is processed for two cents per bushel and then returns the feed to his own property for his own cattle raising purposes, whereas in eastern Canada the farmers support the wheat board and must pay the higher price. The farmers in this area have been sceptical regarding the allowance of this leeway to the feed mills, and have felt that it was detrimental to themselves. When this detriment is reflected in eastern Canada to the extent of 50 cents a bushel for feed grain the farmers certainly feel that they are not getting a fair shake.
Would the hon. member permit another question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.

How does this situation reflect on the economy of the eastern Canadian agriculture situation? The hon. member knows, as a result of his attendance and the attendance of his leader at the meetings of the agriculture committee, that the percentage of grain in western Canada going into feed mills is very limited.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Surely the hon. member will admit that there is a difference in cost in the neighbourhood of 50 cents a bushel. This represents a great difference in the cost of raising cattle as between the two areas. If the difference in cost were only a few cents, then I would admit that there would not be much effect on the cost of production in eastern Canada.
I am familiar with the practices of the feed grain companies in western Canada because they are in fact the same companies

which exist in eastern Canada. I know that these companies are not going to sell the grain for 50 cents less in eastern Canada because they are able to purchase it for 50 cents less in western Canada. There is certainly a relationship between the purchase price and the selling price. If the grain company were to charge the farmers raising cattle in western Canada the same price that the farmers in eastern Canada pay for feed grain, the man in western Canada would not buy from the grain company but would purchase his feed grain from his neighbour.
How does the difference in cost affect the farmer in eastern Canada? I must tell the hon. member that hundreds of head of cattle are sold at community sales each week in my area. The farmers in my area are certainly in competition with the beef producers in western Canada; and if there is to be this great difference in the cost of grain feed then there will certainly be a difference between the price of eastern and the price of western beef. I do not think that situation is difficult to understand.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Has the hon. member any evidence to support his suggestion that the farmer in western Canada sells his feed grain at 50 cents per bushel below the market price?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have it right here.
Put it on the record.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was informed that this is so, and I have no reason to believe it is not so. I am very much surprised at the western members. They are very happy to say that this does not happen, but they must know it has been happening for years and years. There has been a continual bootlegging of grains in western Canada outside the sphere of the wheat board. This has been going on for a long, long time.
Mr. Chairman, I was going to continue my speech on other subjects, but this matter has now been raised and perhaps I should deal with it. The national farmers union presented a brief to the government this year, and in it they had a great deal to say about this matter. I will read some of the brief:
We believe that the family farm is the most efficient unit in terms not only of production, but also in terms of soil conservation and human and social values. We, therefore, believe that the preservation of the family farm is of importance to farm families as well as to the nation as a whole.
6. Reports from local farm forum groups, as publicized by the Saskatchewan farm forum office, indicate that country people were disgruntled by the farm forum guide. One forum ''wished to express their disapproval of the ideas contained
Supply-Agriculture
therein, and would be glad if the person or persons responsible for its contents were not given an opportunity to write for it again". Another forum bluntly stated: ''It looks to us like someone is trying to sell us down the river".
7. We share the dismay of the forums and have brought this information to your attention because it has a direct bearing on our main question which we have put to you in 1959 and 1960, and to which we have not received an answer. The question is:
"Are federal agricultural policies to be enacted that will aim at the preservation of widely distributed private ownership of productive assets, enabling men to maintain themselves and their families on their farms, or does the federal government intend to let those economic forces have free play, that encourage the trend to anonymous, corporate ownership with all its inherent dangers".
Further on in the brief this is said:
9. Still dealing with the question of the family farm v. the factory farm, we draw to your attention the grave effects any weakening of the quota system of the Canadian wheat board will have on the economic position of farmers in the prairies.
Mr. Chairman, will my hon. friend permit another question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly.
Is my hon. friend under the impression that this situation arose this year, last year or the year before? Does he recognize it has been in existence for 20 years-
Never.
-and that we are now legalizing a practice that has grown up over a long period of time?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman; I am well aware of that. I said that bootlegging had gone on for a long time, but bootlegging is not recognized as a favourable practice in my area. We certainly never elected to the House of Commons people who participated in this practice. That happened with the former western member who bootlegged in wheat and demonstrated this fact publicly in advertisements. He is no longer a member of this house. Unfortunately he was a member of this party. He put advertisements in the newspapers which showed he was condoning the bootlegging of wheat.
To answer the hon. member's question, I am well aware that this practice has gone on, and I am not in agreement with legalizing bootlegging.
We had a great deal of talk last year about the unfortunate position of the feed mills. If that was only to legalize bootlegging, I am not in favour of it. Mr. McNamara is not in favour of it either-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I did not use the word "bootlegging". I merely said that a practice had grown up in western Canada by virtue of the dire necessity for a market for wheat. Because of that situation, this practice developed.

I did not use the word "bootlegging" and I had no intention of using it. I resent my hon. friend accusing me of using that word.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not accuse
the hon. member of using it. I used it. I am only using a colloquial expression to describe something that everybody else may call by a much more polite name. Even the government had a name for it, because they put it under legislation and called it something else altogether, assistance to feed mills or something of that nature.
That is nonsense.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If these hon. gentlemen who talk from their seats will rise and ask questions, I will answer them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member would have to obtain the unanimous consent of the house to answer any questions, because his time has expired.
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the belligerence of the hon. member for Timiskaming this evening and the seeming split which has developed in the C.C.F.-New Party-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not at all.

-between the east and the west, pitting the eastern farmer against the western farmer. I must say that this is not the first instance we have seen of this split today. The hon. member for Assiniboia was talking about people going off the farms during our discussion on the previous agricultural resolution and disagreeing strongly with it. Then the hon. member for Timiskaming rose later and said that people should be taken off the farms, large tracts of land should be assembled by the government and these people should manage them as government employees. We have here a complete contradiction in policy and philosophy and I can see a large chasm and great split developing in this small group down at the end of the chamber.
I expect the hon. gentleman wants large, corporate state farms run by state officials. That is the only conclusion I can draw from what he has said. I must point out to the hon. member that if he examines the record tomorrow he will see that earlier today the leader of his group spoke rather differently.
There is one matter to which I would refer specifically this evening. I wish to refer to page 2404 of Hansard of Friday, February 24, 1961, when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were being dealt with. The Minister of Agriculture was dividing up the estimates for this coming season into four main categories. One of these categories was

grants and subsidies, and another was rehabilitation, including P.F.R.A. and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. The third area covered a wide range of legislation under the Canada Grain Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act. The fourth area covered agricultural research within the Department of Agriculture. It is this area specifically with which I should like to deal briefly this evening.
The minister told us that the agricultural research section takes up 24 per cent of the revenue of his department, and as a figure that is $28.8 million for this coming year. This is a large figure, and coupled with the amount expended in provincial agricultural research this must add up to a very considerable figure indeed for research right across Canada.
I have mentioned previously in this house the idea of an agricultural research council in Canada. I should like to develop this idea briefly this evening. I am convinced that such a council could facilitate co-ordination and liaison between the different types of agricultural research in the federal government and its research system, the experimental farm system, and the various provincial agricultural research bodies across Canada. At present there is of course liaison in this field, but I have in mind a body which would report directly to the Minister of Agriculture and which might perhaps be able better to co-ordinate the work and to bring about a focus of attention on areas of agricultural research which might be either too big, too small or too difficult to be covered by any single body set up at the present time.
I also have in mind that while we could get more for the money spent presently in the total field of agricultural research in Canada, we might be able to save money and avoid duplication through overlapping in this field. I should also like to comment briefly on the liaison that exists in this area at the present time. There are at the present time a number of methods of liaison between the federal department of agriculture and the provincial departments and the other agricultural bodies. There are, for instance, associate committees of the national research council sponsored by the national research council and having varied membership. Such committees have dealt in the past with problems of plant breeding, plant diseases and animal nutrition. They are essentially work planning committees or committees planning the co-ordination of research in these various fields. In addition, the provincial governments sponsor committees in various fields. Federal research men sit on these various

committees which are largely concerned with the pooling of information and the dispensing of research information together with its practical results.
Many provinces have these committees. 1 am told the Atlantic provinces share one. I am not certain whether Quebec has one or not. There is also a national advisory committee on agriculture made up of the federal deputy minister and all the provincial deputy ministers of agriculture across Canada. There are certain specific subject subcommittees under the national advisory committee and research personnel sit on these subcommittees. I can point to such examples as the national committee on weeds co-ordinating weed research programs. Other subcommittees deal with animal breeding, farm buildings, engineering, soils, and simi ar subjects. These subcommittees are largely concerned with research planning, but include some extension matters. Also under the national advisory committee is a series of provincial committees, one per province, under the chairmanship, I believe of Mr. A. E. Barrett, assistant to the director general of the research branch of the federal Department of Agriculture. Provincial experts form the remainder of the membership and they study all sorts of fields, mainly extension projects but including new facilities, specific projects and requests from farm bodies and individuals, I am told. There is another form of liaison which goes on at the present time. It takes place at federal agricultural stations such as Harrow, Ontario, and Kentville, Nova Scotia. Here provincial extension men work in co-operation with federal personnel. Liaison of this sort is both right and proper.
I said earlier that I believe the setting up of an agricultural research council would mean better use being made of the money and personnel now being devoted to this field by both federal and provincial governments. I should now like to comment briefly on the organization of such a council in Great Britain at the present time. I am examining a document entitled "The Promotion of the Sciences in the Commonwealth" put out by the United Kingdom information office in January, 1958. The publication notes that agricultural research in its early days in Britain was not centrally organized. We know of such important stations as the Rothamsted experimental station which, I believe, was originally set up privately around 1889. Some 20 years later, in 1909 it was recommended that financial aid should be made available from the development fund to aid and develop agriculture and rural industries by promoting scientific research. In 1911 the development fund was used to promote a scheme which led to the establishment of many of
Supply-Agriculture
the present day agricultural institutions. In 1931, in Britain, the agricultural research council was established by royal charter to be responsible for the general organization and development of agricultural research in Britain.
The council was given funds to spend at its own direction and gradually took over the various responsibilities in this field. I will go on to say that it is responsible in Great Britain to a committee of the privy council for agricultural research, and under the agricultural research act of 1956 it was charged with the organization and development of agricultural research at which time an agricultural research fund was established. This council consists of not more than 18 and no fewer than 15 members. It is of varied composition and it is responsible for the financing of independent research institutes and-this is very interesting-for making grants for special investigations to universities and research bodies. It also awards research fellowships and post-graduate studentships in agricultural and veterinary science. There is obviously great co-ordination there but of course we must not draw the immediate conclusion that we need exactly the same system here in Canada. I would only say that in a country such as Canada with its provincial jurisdictions and a much wider area to be covered, the establishment of such a council might prove even more advantageous.
I should now like to point out briefly what happens in the United States. The situation there is different but there is considerable liaison between the federal government in Washington and the various state governments. I am quoting from a document put out by the national science foundation and entitled "Organization of the Federal Government for scientific Activities". This publication states on page 23:
While most scientific activities are carried out by the department with its own personnel and its own facilities a significant proportion is conducted through co-operative, contractual and grant programs with state and private institutions and agencies, and with industrial firms. The unique and central feature of the research programs of the department is its traditional system of elaborate co-operation and co-ordination with the research and educational activities of the land-grant colleges of the states and territories of the union.
We can see that there is a very fair measure of co-operation and liaison there.
In conclusion I should like to define a little more clearly what I think an agricultural research council could do in Canada. I believe it could define research problems. It could define them jointly, given good liaison, with all those working in this particular field in Canada. Second, in solving the problem, for

Supply-Agriculture
instance, it could work through universities, through provincial or federal research establishments depending perhaps on the background the availability and personnel and so forth to work on any given problem. It could perhaps also work jointly with private companies in the agricultural research field. The membership of such a council would include, I suppose, provincial and federal representation, farm groups and companies involved in the agricultural business and research field. I would say that such a council might not at first undertake its own research projects. It could perhaps recommend initially at least to various bodies that various projects should be conducted and could go slow at first with the actual allocation or spending of moneys on its own. After it got going it might adopt some more basic functions and be able to allocate money with regard to specific areas and difficulties in the agricultural research field. This council could examine areas where Canada at present has blank spots. It might direct its attention to problems too big or too difficult, or too small or too specific to be undertaken at other levels. It could indicate how joint action, joint co-ordination and co-operation might solve such problems and then could allocate funds to a specific research group attached to an agricultural college, university or other such institutions.
I have emphasized that such a council might save us money. I am convinced it could do away with overlapping and duplication and could focus attention on the real problems facing agriculture today. It would aid in the education and training of our scientists and personnel engaged in this field. I believe that the retired secretary of the agricultural research council in Britain, Sir William Slater, has made a study relating to re-organization within our own Department of Agriculture. Perhaps such a man might be called upon to make recommendations concerning whether or not an agricultural research council should be set up in Canada, and indeed he may have done so.
There is another matter that is related to this field that probably could come under such a council or perhaps could be set up separately. I refer to the national council on farm policy research which is to be held in Winnipeg in April, 1961. This council has to do with marketing problems and economic policies. It therefore is somewhat outside the ambit of the research field of which I am speaking and perhaps it might be wiser not to combine with research the political aspect, and the controversial field of economics and marketing problems. Perhaps consideration would be given to the establishment of what would be strictly a research council.

Mr. Chairman, I hope these ideas will be given favourable consideration by the government in the future.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the previous speaker for his intervention. I wish to remind him of one thing of which he should be reminded and to which he should give consideration. The hon. gentleman made a reference to my leader and myself and our views in respect of this present measure. I wish to inform the hon. gentleman, through you, Mr. Chairman, that I was elected by the people in the constituency of Timiskaming to come to parliament to represent them to the best of my ability, always having their interests at heart. It does not apply in this case but let me say I would stand up for the interests of the people of my riding against any hon. member in any part of the chamber. My prime responsibility is to those who elected me. I am not like some of the hon. gentleman's colleagues who say, in effect, "We would love to do this but our party is against it at this time". If the hon. gentleman wants quotations, I have them here and with the permission of the Chair I will read them. What the hon. member's party stands for is the exact opposite of what we stand for.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have not read the quotation and if there is objection I will not do so.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member had his time a little while ago. Is the hon. gentleman now making another speech?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is entitled to speak for 30 minutes at a time.
And as often as he likes.
The Tories have not yet applied closure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was saying that I support my riding, my people and their interests and if it is necessary I will do so against any segment of the committee. In this instance there is no difference of opinion. Now that this issue has been raised there will be a further statement. Previously it had not been raised. I thank the hon. member for Moose Jaw, Dauphin, Medicine Hat or wherever he comes from, for raising it in the first place.
Hon. members of the Conservative party do not represent their ridings but vote as the government decides they should vote or as the cabinet suggests. Here is a statement made by one hon. member of the government party:

We are torn, as it were, between two choices, like a lather with two sons. If a recommendation has been made by the cabinet, or by the minister, and apparently it has been, I submit that the government members have no alternative other than to support our government.
Would the hon. member state from what he is reading?
The hon. member does not know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am reading from the evidence of the standing committee on veterans affairs of February 23, 1961. If hon. members wish me to do so, I will name the people.
I believe it is customary under the rules of the committee for an hon. member to state what he is reading from and to indicate who made the statement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The first statement was made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, is it proper for an hon. member to read from a document of that kind when the committee is sitting and has not reported?
In any event, what does this have to do with agriculture?
Nothing.
The hon. member is incapable of relating two ideas.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member is reading from the proceedings of the committee on agriculture and colonization?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The veterans affairs committee of this year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that one may quote from a report of a committee but that one may not criticize a decision taken by a committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
At page 126 of this report the hon. member for Megantic is reported to have said:
Our responsibility is to study the bill and to make the best decision we can on it. The only power that we have is to recommend to the government. And now, it is up to the members, whether they are supporting the government or the opposition, to make their positions clear. After our position is made known to the house, it is up to the government to decide as to whether it implements the recommendations or not. Then, at that time, the members can vote for the government or against it. It is as simple as that.
On the same page, the hon. member for Middlesex West is reported as saying:
I will be glad to make my statement without political bias. However, it is a fact that the members of the government are placed in an awkward position.
Supply-Agriculture
The awkward position is that government members were not representing the veterans in their constituency because the government was not taking action in the particular matter under consideration. The hon. members of the government had to vote against the wishes of the people who elected them because the Conservative party said that was what they had to do. The government did not accept the recommendations presented.
I refer to this matter in order to make it clear that I will vote against my party when it is necessary to do so in the interests of my constituents.
When have you ever done it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have done so on a number of occasions; and to be completely fair I should say that this has been done on a number of occasions by hon. members of the party to which the hon. member who raised the matter belongs. Of course they got into trouble for doing so, but they exercised their integrity and sincerity on those occasions.
I return now to the question of the wheat board with which subject I was dealing when I was so rudely interrupted by the expiry of my time.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would the hon. member ask his leader what he finds so funny? The hon. member for Assiniboia has been sitting there giggling for the last half hour.
I have been looking at you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not need to ask him. What is funny is that a government member should ask questions that are so easily refuted. Let me read the refutation advanced by the wheat board:
Chief Commissioner W. C. McNamara pinpointed the operation of the Canadian wheat board before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization when he said:
"Orderly marketing is achieved by the quota regulations under the Canadian Wheat Board Act."
He went on to say:
"In the view of our board the essential feature of the marketing scheme established by the statute is the equitable rationing of delivery opportunities and the ensuring that, as far as possible, all producers will get the same basic price at the same time for like kind, grade and quantity of grain. Equal delivery opportunity is the basic feature of the scheme.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, this is not happening. When the price drops 50 cents at the feed mills in so far as one farmer is concerned, another one may be getting a much higher or even a lower price for selling to another feed mill, say, under the wheat board.

Supply-Agriculture
The brief goes on to say:
It is our considered opinion that the recent exemption of western feed mills from the quota and pricing regulations of the Canadian wheat board destroys this "basic feature" of the marketing scheme by depriving many grain producers of equal delivery opportunities.
I am concerned not only with the matter of equal delivery opportunities but also with Mr. McNamara's contention that all producers will get the same basic price at the same time for like kind, grade and quantity of grain. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this feature has been eliminated. I suggest further that its elimination is detrimental to the farmers of eastern Canada. Therefore, I would advise western members to walk very softly when they attack the position that some of us in eastern Canada take, because we have been willing to give them every possible opportunity to get what they desired. We should also like to have that opportunity extended to our farmers. You have noted my support on many occasions, Mr. Chairman, of the maintenance of stable prices in the legislation which has been introduced, and in measures which have not been introduced. I have supported them because I thought they were better than the measures which were supported by the government members, and I refer particularly to deficiency payments on grain.
Mr. McNamara went on to say:
If a producer may sell a portion of his crop to a mill for flour, feed or seed, outside of his quota, he would then be able to deliver to the other channels of the marketing system grain up to the amount of his quota and thus achieve an advantage over less fortunate producers who were not able to get their grain into the local flour, feed and seed outlets.
In our meeting with the Canadian wheat board at Winnipeg on February 1, Mr. McNamara was questioned and admitted that quotas would be affected by the present exemption of western feed mills.
On a point of order, the hon. gentleman is reading from another document but he has not identified it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sorry; this was a complete oversight. I identified it previously as the national farm union submission to the Canadian government on February 15, 1961.
The hon. gentleman used the word "we".
Presumably they did.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It could be the identity of myself. I continue with the brief:
Finally we want to point out that, when he was asked by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort at the hearing before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization whether he wanted any of the board's powers relaxed, Mr. McNamara said "no".

In view of the chief commissioner's clearly expressed opposition to the exemption of western feed mills from the quota and pricing regulations of the wheat board, the gross injustice it does to many farmers, and the strong sentiments expressed in many country meetings, we respectfully request that the Canadian wheat board be instructed to rescind instructions to the trade Nos. 41 and 43 which allow feed mills open market rights in purchasing feed grain supplies outside of wheat board price and quota regulations. We are happy to report that Mr. McNamara has agreed to meet with our executive and review the situation.
My argument in relation to this matter is that a differential of 50 cents would be detrimental to the beef producers, the poultry producers, the hog producers, the dairy producers, and all those who are buying feed. It would be detrimental to the production of agricultural products in my area because none of this 50 cents will ever flow from the feed mill to my area. None of this 50 cents will ever accrue to the farmers in my riding. If there is a differential in the production of beef and agricultural products which is brought about by the difference of 50 cents in so far as the eastern and western farmers are concerned, it will be the result of legislation passed by this government last year.
I hope this matter will go before the agriculture committee. I hope this will be referred to that committee by the minister who no doubt is aware of this situation because he represents all the farmers of Canada and not only one small segment, namely the grain producers.
Small?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This matter has to be incorporated in the regulations of the wheat board. We in eastern Canada want the equality that existed under the wheat board to be extended to us.
There will be no difference of opinion between my leader and myself in this regard. He is now the leader of a very influential party in Canada. He will speak on behalf of the farmers of western Canada with the same strong voice as that with which he has spoken before. He will also ask them to give respect and consideration to the needs and desires of the farmers in my area as well as those of all other farmers throughout Canada. In the C.C.F. we have always had a leader who has been willing to speak for all the people of Canada, as, incidentally, it is the responsibility of every member in this house to do.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

No; you cannot chisel like that.
Progress reported.
I believe the house leader intends to indicate some slight change in the business for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. Following consultation with the parties on the other side of the house, it now appears that it would be appropriate to start off with interim supply tomorrow. My understanding is that we hope that by one o'clock interim supply would be completed. Then we would follow with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
The forecast for next week, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, runs in this way, subject, of course, to change and to the progress that the house makes. We will start off on Monday
Business of the House with supplementary estimates. It is impossible to tell how long we shall be on those, but during the course of the three days we should like also to consider Bill No. S-5, which is No. 1 on today's order paper, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, and Bill No. S-6, which follows it, to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act. These bills were before the house earlier and were referred to the banking and commerce committee. They have now come back to the house. If time permits next week, we might also continue with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

subtopic: FEDERAL GRANTS FOR AIRPORT CONSTRUCTION, QUEBEC
FEDERAL GRANTS FOR AIRPORT CONSTRUCTION, QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of Transport made any grant for the construction or extension of the following airports: Baie Comeau, Gaspe, Godbout, Havre St. Pierre, Matane, Rimouski, Rouyn, St. Jean, and Senneterre?
2.	Are the said airports placed under municipal management?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport):
1 and 2. The department has made grants in aid toward construction at the airports at Gaspe, Matane, Rouyn, Senneterre and Havre St. Pierre. In addition, the department has
actually carried out construction work at airports at Rimouski, St. Jean and Baie Comeau.

subtopic: SUMAS PRAIRIE, B.C.    PURCHASE OF LAND FOR AIRPORT
SUMAS PRAIRIE, B.C.    PURCHASE OF LAND FOR AIRPORT
speechtext:
1.	Did the federal government in or about the year 1940 purchase land on the Sumas prairie in British Columbia for the construction of an airport?
2.	H so, what was the amount of land purchased, and total price paid for same?
3.	Has the federal government sold all or any part of this land, and, if so, to whom, and for what price?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport):
1 and 2. Yes, in 1942, the Department of Transport, acting as agent for the Department of National Defence, acquired by expropriation approximately 422 acres of land, at a total cost of $32,624.30.
3. Yes, all the land was sold in 1958, through Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, to Buckersfield's Ltd., of Vancouver, B.C., for the price of $67,601.

Friday, March 24, 1961
